lessons.title: Plant and animal cells
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Biology — Cell structure: plant and animal cells, organelles, magnification (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original text written for the GCE O Level Biology syllabus; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the main organelles of plant and animal cells and state their functions.
State the differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.
Label a cell diagram and calculate magnification or actual size.

blocks.title: The cell
blocks.md:
The **cell** is the basic unit of structure and function of all living organisms. Most cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye, so we study them with a **light microscope**.

The small structures inside a cell, each with its own job, are called **organelles**.

blocks.title: Structures found in both plant and animal cells
blocks.md:
- **Nucleus**: contains the chromosomes (DNA) and controls the activities of the cell.
- **Cell membrane**: partially permeable; controls what enters and leaves the cell.
- **Cytoplasm**: jelly-like fluid where most chemical reactions take place.
- **Mitochondria**: site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy.
- **Ribosomes**: site of protein synthesis.

blocks.title: Structures found only in plant cells
blocks.md:
- **Cell wall** made of **cellulose**: fully permeable; gives the cell a fixed shape and support.
- **Chloroplasts**: contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.
- **Large permanent vacuole** filled with **cell sap**: keeps the cell firm (turgid).

Animal cells have no cell wall, no chloroplasts and at most small, temporary vacuoles. They store carbohydrate as **glycogen**; plant cells store **starch**.

blocks.caption: A typical plant (palisade) cell as seen under the light microscope.
blocks.alt: A rectangular plant cell: a thick green cell wall, a thin cell membrane inside it, a large blue vacuole in the centre, a nucleus in the cytoplasm on the left and several small green chloroplasts.

blocks.caption: A typical animal cell (for example a cheek cell): no cell wall, no chloroplasts, no large vacuole.
blocks.alt: A rounded animal cell surrounded only by a cell membrane, with a large nucleus near the centre and two small orange mitochondria in the cytoplasm.

blocks.title: Magnification
blocks.md: Image size and actual size must be in the **same unit** before dividing. Remember: 1 mm = 1000 µm (micrometres). Magnification has **no unit**; write it as ×400, for example.

blocks.title: Method: magnification questions
blocks.md:
1. Measure the image (drawing or photo) with a ruler, in mm.
2. Convert both lengths to the same unit (usually µm: multiply mm by 1000).
3. Write the formula, rearranged if needed: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
4. Substitute, calculate, and give the unit (none for magnification, µm or mm for a size).

blocks.title: Worked example 1: identify a cell from a diagram
blocks.statement: The diagram shows a cell seen under a light microscope. Name the parts A, B, C and D, and state, with two reasons, whether it is a plant cell or an animal cell.

steps.md: A is the thick outer layer: the **cell wall**. B is a small green body: a **chloroplast**.
C is the large central space: the **vacuole** (containing cell sap). D is the rounded body in the cytoplasm: the **nucleus**.
Animal cells never have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts or a large permanent vacuole. This cell has all three.
Two reasons are enough for full marks, for example: it has a **cell wall** and it has **chloroplasts**.

blocks.answer: **A = cell wall, B = chloroplast, C = vacuole, D = nucleus. It is a plant cell: it has a cell wall and chloroplasts (and a large vacuole).**

blocks.title: Worked example 2: calculate a magnification
blocks.statement: In a textbook photograph, a human cheek cell measures 24 mm across. The real cell is 60 µm across. Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

steps.md: Put both lengths in the same unit. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so the image size is:
Magnification has no unit: we write **×400**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that plant cells have a cell wall **instead of** a cell membrane: they have **both**.
- Calling the cell wall partially permeable: it is **fully** permeable; the membrane is partially permeable.
- Thinking every plant cell has chloroplasts: root cells and onion bulb cells have none.
- Dividing lengths in different units (mm by µm).
- Giving magnification a unit, such as "400 mm".

items: Cells were first named by Robert Hooke in 1665 after he looked at thin slices of cork, which reminded him of the small rooms (cells) of monks.
An electron microscope magnifies far more than a light microscope and shows details such as ribosomes and the inner membranes of mitochondria.

reviewNotes: Check whether the current syllabus expects ribosomes and mitochondria at this level (they are only clearly visible with an electron microscope).

exercises.prompt: Which organelle absorbs light energy for photosynthesis?
exercises.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy used in photosynthesis. Mitochondria release energy by respiration.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Match each cell structure with its function.
pairs: Controls the activities of the cell
Controls what enters and leaves the cell
Gives the plant cell support and a fixed shape
exercises.explanation: Nucleus: control (it contains the DNA). Cell membrane: partially permeable barrier. Mitochondrion: aerobic respiration. Cell wall: cellulose layer for support. Ribosome: protein synthesis.
exercises.method: Link each structure to a single key verb: control, regulate entry, release energy, support, make proteins.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: True or false: an animal cell is surrounded by a cell wall made of cellulose.
exercises.explanation: False. Only plant cells (and some other organisms) have a cellulose cell wall. An animal cell is surrounded only by its cell membrane.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: A student draws an onion epidermal cell 36 mm long. The actual length of the cell is 0.09 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing (give the number only).
exercises.explanation: Both lengths are already in mm: magnification = 36 ÷ 0.09 = 400. The drawing is ×400.
exercises.method: Check that both lengths are in the same unit, then divide image size by actual size.
mistakes: Dividing the actual size by the image size (0.09 ÷ 36 = 0.0025).
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: On a photograph taken at a magnification of ×500, a guard cell measures 15 mm long. Calculate its actual length in micrometres (µm).
exercises.explanation: Image size = 15 mm = 15 000 µm. Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 15 000 ÷ 500 = 30 µm.
exercises.method: Rearrange the formula: actual size = image size ÷ magnification, then convert mm to µm (× 1000).
mistakes: Forgetting to convert: 15 ÷ 500 = 0.03 is in mm, not µm.
Multiplying by the magnification instead of dividing.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: The diagram shows a cell taken from the lining of a student's mouth, drawn at a magnification of ×800.
exercises.method: Read the whole question first; in calculations, write the formula, the substitution and the unit.
mistakes: Giving only one difference when two are asked for.
Forgetting to convert mm to µm.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.explanation: P is the large rounded body in the cytoplasm of this animal cell: the nucleus. A cheek cell has no chloroplasts and no cell wall.

parts.prompt: Structure Q is a mitochondrion. What is its function?
choices: It releases energy by aerobic respiration
It controls the entry of substances
parts.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy from glucose.

parts.prompt: State two ways in which a palisade cell of a leaf differs from this cell.
parts.model: The palisade cell has a cellulose cell wall; it has chloroplasts; it has a large permanent vacuole containing cell sap. (Any two.)
rubric: 1 mark for each correct difference, maximum 2.
The answer must say what the plant cell HAS (or the cheek cell lacks): "different shape" alone scores 0.
parts.explanation: Plant cells have three structures that animal cells lack: a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole.

parts.prompt: The diameter of the cell on the drawing is 48 mm. Calculate the actual diameter of the cell in µm.

exercises.prompt: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
exercises.explanation: The cellulose cell wall is found only in plant cells; the other three are found in both.

exercises.prompt: Which structure contains the genetic material (DNA) of the cell?
exercises.explanation: The chromosomes, made of DNA, are in the nucleus.

exercises.prompt: The cell membrane is described as partially permeable. This means that it...
choices: lets some substances through but not others
exercises.explanation: A partially permeable membrane controls entry and exit: it allows some molecules through and not others.

exercises.prompt: An image is 20 mm long and the object is 0.1 mm long. What is the magnification?
In which form do animal cells store carbohydrate?
exercises.explanation: Animal cells store glycogen; plant cells store starch. Cellulose builds plant cell walls.

exercises.prompt: Question 1 — Cells (4 marks). A student observes cells from a cassava leaf and from a human cheek under a light microscope.
exercises.method: Show the formula and the unit conversion in the calculation.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: Which structure controls the substances that enter and leave both types of cell?
parts.explanation: The partially permeable cell membrane controls entry and exit. The cell wall is fully permeable and is absent from the cheek cell.

parts.prompt: A leaf cell 0.12 mm long appears 48 mm long in the student's drawing. Calculate the magnification of the drawing (number only).
parts.explanation: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 48 ÷ 0.12 = 400, so ×400 (1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the answer).

parts.prompt: True or false: both the leaf cell and the cheek cell contain mitochondria.
parts.explanation: True. Plant cells respire too, so they contain mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.
